summary: A correction to BBN Report 1822: a page was wrong about when a host is marked dead. In fact the timeout has always been 30 seconds and the host was never marked dead under the stated conditions. This is an error in the report, not a change to the IMP system.

eli5.summary: A fix to a manual: the manual had one number wrong, but the machine had always worked as it should.

questions: how does imp detect dead hosts
subtitle: Correction to a documentation error about IMP host timeout.

tldr.problem: BBN Report No. 1822, which documents the IMP system, contains an error on page 25 about when a host is marked dead.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 270 provides a corrected page showing the actual timeout is 30 seconds, not 40, and clarifies that the host is NOT marked dead under the stated conditions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC clarifies that the IMP system itself was always correct; only the documentation was wrong.

today: RFC 270 is not Internet Standard. It is a historical document showing how documentation errors in early systems were corrected. The host timeout behavior it describes was specific to the IMP system, which has been obsolete since the early 1980s when the network transitioned to TCP/IP.

sections.title: The Error
sections.content:
Alex McKenzie at BBN discovered errors in BBN Report No. 1822 while preparing RFC 271. The report documents the IMP (Interface Message Processor) system and how it handles host communication. The primary error is on page 25, which incorrectly states that a host is marked dead under certain timeout conditions.

McKenzie's team identified the need for a corrected version of page 25 and also required deletion of the first two lines of page 26. The changes show that the host is NOT marked dead under the stated conditions and that the timeout period is 30 seconds, not 40 seconds.
sections.eli5: The manual said the machine waits 40 seconds before deciding a host is dead. It actually waits 30, and even then the host does not get marked dead the way the manual said.

sections.title: Documentation, Not System Change
sections.content:
Critically, McKenzie emphasizes that these changes reflect errors in previous versions of Report 1822, not changes to the IMP system itself. The IMP has ALWAYS used a 30-second timeout and the host was NEVER marked dead under the stated conditions. The actual hardware and software were correct all along.

This is a pure documentation correction. The document had drifted from reality, and RFC 270 helps bring it back in line with how the system actually operates. A more formal update to Report 1822 was promised for distribution later.
sections.eli5: The machine always worked right. Someone just wrote down the wrong numbers in the manual.

sections.title: Significance
sections.content:
RFC 270 is brief but important: it shows how early network documentation could become inaccurate. BBN Report No. 1822 was the authoritative specification for IMP behavior, but humans writing documentation can misstate how systems actually work.

The RFC process, by making corrections public and linked to earlier documents, helped catch and fix such errors. Sites relying on Report 1822 for implementing their host software would have been confused without this clarification.
sections.eli5: This small note helped people understand the real behavior, stopping them from building wrong things based on bad docs.

sections.title: Scope
sections.content:
RFC 270 exemplifies how the early RFC process handled errata and clarifications. Rather than waiting for a complete new edition of a report, corrections could be published quickly as RFCs, ensuring all network sites received the right information promptly.

The emphasis on clarity—that this is a documentation correction, not a system change—shows good practice. It prevents unnecessary alarm and confusion among implementers and operators.
sections.eli5: When docs are wrong, fix them fast and tell everyone. This was how the early network kept information reliable.

references.text: BBN, "The ARPANET Imp Program Quarterly Technical Report", BBN Report No. 1822, NIC 7958, 1970.
